items.source_title: Fixr, Cost to Build an Attached Garage (updated Aug 29, 2025)
items.note: Commercial cost-guide estimate, NOT an authoritative or government source. It covers adding a garage (24x24 two-car garage, vinyl siding, asphalt roof, unfinished interior), not a garage built with a new home. Fixr's national average is $37,000 (range $23,000-$45,000); prefab is $40-$60/sq ft. No authoritative public source (NAHB, Census, ICC) for garage $/sq ft or a garage-to-living-space cost ratio was found.

items.source_title: not found
items.note: Not found in any authoritative public source. Any ratio would be a derivation by the app, for example Fixr's $60-80 divided by NAHB's $162 gives about 0.37-0.49, mixing two unrelated sources. Label it as such if you use it.

items.source_title: not found
items.note: No authoritative national source gives 'typical' single-family setbacks, height, or lot coverage. These are set by each local zoning ordinance. A 35 ft height cap is common in many local codes, but no national standard or survey confirming it was verified. If used, label as illustrative, user-adjustable defaults.

items.source_title: International Residential Code (2015-2024 editions), Section R304.1 Minimum area; as applied in City of Seattle SDCI Code Solution 'SRC Section R304.1 & R304.2 Habitable Room Size' (Oct 2017)
items.note: Code text: 'Habitable rooms shall have a floor area of not less than 70 square feet.' Exception: kitchens. Confirmed through the Seattle government interpretation and secondary quotes of the 2021 IRC. The official ICC text (codes.iccsafe.org) blocked automated fetching (HTTP 403), so it was not read directly. In 2012 and earlier editions this rule was numbered R304.2.

items.source_title: International Residential Code (2015-2024 editions), Section R304.2 Minimum dimensions; City of Seattle SDCI Code Solution (Oct 2017)
items.note: Code text: 'Habitable rooms shall be not less than 7 feet in any horizontal dimension.' Exception: kitchens. Seattle's reading: 'Only portions of the room in which a 7 foot by 7-foot square can be placed are allowed to be counted toward the habitable space requirement.' In 2012 and earlier editions this rule was numbered R304.3.

state_factor_source.title: UFS 3-701-01 DoD Facilities Pricing Guide, Table 4-1 CONUS Area Cost Factors (MILCON 'AREA COST FACTOR' column), from the 2026 Data Tables workbook
state_factor_source.edition: UFS 3-701-01, 6 June 2026 (data tables dated 06-06-2026; based on CONUS market surveys conducted in 2025)
state_factor_source.how_derived: Table 4-1 CONUS lists about 15,500 DoD sites with a MILCON Area Cost Factor and has no state-average rows. For each state and DC: (1) group sites by Installation Code, (2) take each installation's most common (modal) ACF as its main entry, (3) take the low median of those installation values (statistics.median_low), so every published factor is a value that appears in the DoD table and no new numbers are made by averaging. 'District Of Columbia' and 'District of Columbia' spellings were merged. NO re-normalization was applied. Per UFS section 4-1.2, ACFs are already normalized so the 96-Base-City average (two base cities per contiguous state) = 1.00, which is close to, but not exactly, a population-weighted US average. CAVEATS: (a) ACFs model a military-construction market basket (MLE ratio 63/35/2, plus weather, seismic, labor availability, logistics, and productivity factors), not residential construction; (b) UFS 4-1.1 says MILCON ACFs 'should not be applied or utilized for any other purpose' than DoD construction cost estimating, so using them for houses is an approximation the app must disclose; (c) Alaska (2.25) and Hawaii (2.13) reflect remote-installation logistics and probably overstate typical residential premiums there; (d) factors reflect where military installations are, not population-weighted state averages.
